questionStem: A 25-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of growths on her lips and tongue for severa l years. Examination shows nodules on the lips, buccal mucosa, and tongue; cafe au lait spots over the trunk and limbs; and scattered nodules on the skin. This patient is at greatest risk for which of the following conditions?
correctExplanation: Mucosa! neuromas, growths on the oral mucosa and lips, are a finding of multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) type 2B. Other features of MEN2B include medullary thyroid carcinoma, and pheochromocytoma. MEN2B is also associated with neurofibromatosis type I, and these disorders can present simultaneous ly. Neurofibromatosis type I (von Recklinghausen disease) is a genetical ly inherited disorder caused by a defect in NF1, the gene which encodes neurofibromin on chromosome 17. It follows an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance. It is characterized by a constellation of cutaneous manifestations (neurofibromas, plexiform neurofibromas, cafe au lait macules, and axillary freckling), a variety of central nervous system tumors including optic nerve glioma and iris hamartoma (Lisch nodule), and bony abnorma lities such as long bone dysplasia and sphenoid wing dysplasia. Patients are also at higher risk for developing astrocytomas, brainstem gliomas, and soft tissue sarcomas. Neurofibromatosis type II has a different constellation of findings: bilateral acoustic schwannomas, cataracts, meningiomas, and ependymomas, and is not associated with MEN.

Lymphoma (Choice C) is a hematologic malignancy derived from lymphocytes which has many different subtypes and presentations. CNS lymphoma is a type of intracranial neoplasm, but it is not seen in neurofibromatosis type I or MEN2B. questionStem: A 57-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of gradually progressive weakness in the shoulder and hip muscles. She has hypothyroidism treated with thyroxine but is otherw ise healthy. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Neurologic examinat ion shows moderate bilatera l weakness of the deltoid, biceps, triceps, psoas, glutei, and quadr iceps muscles. The remainder of the examinat ion shows no abnormalities. Her erythrocyte sedimentat ion rate is 85 mm/h, and serum creatine kinase activity is 2456 U/L. Complete blood count and urinalysis are within normal limits. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.B: Electromyograp hy and nerve conduction studies

correctExplanation: Electromyography and nerve conduction studies are used to support a diagnosis of inflammatory myopathy such as polymyositis, as in this case. Polymyositis is an autoimmune condition affecting the proximal muscles. It is closely related to dermatomyositis, however, unlike dermatomyositis, it does not present with cutaneous findings. The muscular inflamma tion is characterized by endomysial COB+ inflamma tory infiltrate. This is in contrast to dermatomyositis which demonstrates a perimysial CD4+ inflammato ry infiltrate. An inflamma tory infiltrate of the muscle occurs, causing damage to the myocytes, leading to release of creatine kinase, an intracellular molecule. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate is also increased, indicating the presence of inflammation. This can be used to monitor disease progress in polymyositis. Both polymyositis and dermatomyositis are characterized by several autoantibodies: positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) and anti-Jo-1, anti-SRP, and anti-Mi-2. Treatment of polymyositis involves systemic steroids followed by long-term immunosuppressive therapy with medications such as methotrexate or azathioprine.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Quantitative sensory testing (Choice A) is used to evaluate damage to small and large nerve endings, not primary muscle inflammation. MRI of the spinal cord (Choice C) would be beneficial in evaluating muscle weakness because of a spinal epidural abscess or tumor. While these pathologies can cause proximal muscle weakness, other symptoms such as feve r, back pain, and sensory deficits would also be seen. As polymyositis is an inflammatory myopathy with no spinal cord involvement, imaging of the spinal cord will not be helpful. Skin biopsy (Choice D) is indicated in evaluation of suspected dermatomyositis. However, this patient does not demonstrate any cutaneous findings, and thus, a skin biopsy is not warranted.

questionStem: A 27-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department because of multip le trauma sustained in a motor vehicle collision. He is initially arousable, but he is increasingly unrespons ive over the next 45 minutes. The pupil of the left eye is dilated, and there is ptosis of the left eyelid. He begins to hyperve ntilate. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

choices.B: Aseptic meningitis H) I nfratentorial lesion
choices.D: Carbon monoxide poisoning J) Salicy late intoxication
choices.E: Centra l herniation K) Uncal herniation

correctExplanation: After blunt head injury, patients can present with concussion or traumatic intracranial hemorrhage such as subdu ral hematoma, subarachnoid hemorrhage, or epidural hematoma. A young patient with initial normal mental status that then becomes altered or unresponsive raises suspicion for an epidural hematoma. Epidural hematoma is classically associated with trauma to the middle meningeal artery and can present with an initial lucid interva l followed by deterioration of mental status caused by arterial bleeding and hematoma expansion. Over time , patients can have symptoms of headache, vomiting , confusion, seizures, and coma. Epidural hematomas present on CT as lens-shaped, biconvex hyperdense collec tions abutting the skull. They often compress adjacent brain and are bound by dural sutures. Epidural hematoma can be complicated by increased intracranial pressure, midline shift, uncal herniation, and death. Uncal herniation involves the uncus comp ressing the midbrain, typically affecting the oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve Ill), causing pupillary dilation, ptosis, and oculomotor nerve palsy. Emergent craniotomy and decompression of the epidural hematoma is often necessary.
incorrectExplanation: nd L. Alcohol withdrawal (Choice A) presents with tremulousness, nausea, vomiting, anxiety, and tongue fasciculations. Delirium tremens is a life-threatening comp lication of alcohol withdrawal that presents with severe confusion, agitation, visua l hallucinations, and autonomic instability. Aseptic meningitis (Choice B), bacterial meningitis (Choice C), and viral meningitis (Choice L) typically present with fever, headache, and nucha l rigidity. This patient has no signs of meningitis and his altered menta l status is more likely because of blunt head trauma. Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning (Choice D) occurs as a consequence of inhaling the gas. CO has an affinity for hemog lobin that is hundreds of times greater than that of oxygen, readily displacing oxygen from heme. Symptoms of CO poisoning include headache, loss of consciousness, dizziness, vomiting, and fatigue.

questionStem: One day after undergo ing an elective cholecystectomy, a 67-year-o ld woman becomes confused and belligerent. She has a 2-year history of mild dementia, Alzheimer type . She takes no medications. Intramusc ular haloperidol is administered, and 1 hour later, she begins to repetitive ly hyperextend her neck. She also has repetitive conjugate upward movements of the eyes that she says she cannot control. Exam ination shows no other abnorma lities. Admin istration of a medication with which of the following properties is the most appropriate treatment?
correctExplanation: Acute dystonias can occur in response to antipsychotics, such as haloperidol, antiepileptic drugs, or antiemetics. Common presentations include torticollis (head tilted to the side and down), retrocollis (head tilted back) , opisthotonos (arching of the back), and oculogyric crisis (upward deviation of the eyes). It rarely presents with laryngospasm and strider. These movements are involuntary and cannot be controlled by the patient. The pathophysiology is an imbalance in the dopaminergic-cholinergic pathways of the basal ganglia. Risk factors for development include male sex, young age, recent cocaine use, and a history of previous acute dystonic reaction. Acute dystonias are treated with diphenhydramine or benztropine, both of which are anticholinergic medications that work to restore the proper balance in the dopaminergic and cholinergic pathways.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Antidopaminergic (Choice B) agents are used primarily in the treatment of schizophrenia and include agents such as haloperidol. Antidopaminergic agents can also be used to treat nausea. As acute dystonias are caused by an imbalance in the dopaminergic and cholinergic pathways, further antagonism of dopamine would likely worsen symptoms. Antiserotonergic (Choice C) medications are used to treat nausea, especially chemotherapy-induced nausea and emesis. Some antidepressants and antipsychotics also have antiserotonergic activity. However, serotonin is not involved in the pathophysiology of acute dystonia. Cholinergic (Choice D) agents increase the amount of acetylcholine present in the neuromuscular junction, which leads to increased muscular contraction. They can be used to treat myasthenia gravis, to reverse neuromuscular blockade, and to improve symptoms associated with Alzheimer disease. Choliner ic a ents would worsen this atient's acute d stonia.

questionStem: A previous ly healthy 32-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of progressive sensory loss. Initially, only her feet felt numb, but the loss of sensation has slowly ascended symmetrica lly to the umbilicus. She also has had urinary urgency and freque ncy, nocturia, and the perception of a tight band-like sensation around her midabdom inal region. Examination shows slowing of left eye adduction during saccad ic movement of the eyes to the right. There is diffuse hyperref lexia. Sensation to pinprick is decreased to the level of the umbilicus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Multiple sclerosis, the most prevalent immune-mediated demyelinating disease, may present initially with transverse myelitis though can also demonstrate neurologic symptoms from lesions in other central nervous system (CNS) locations. Transverse myelitis refers to inflammation that extends transversely across the spinal cord, leading to bilateral sensory, motor, or autonomic dysfunction. When sensory tracts are involved, sensory deficits are evident at a clear dermatomal level (also known as a sensory level, likely T10 in this patient) and may present as a band-like sensation at that level. Autonomic symptoms may present as urinary urgency or incontinence, bowel incontinence, or sexual dysfunction. According to the McDonald criteria for multiple sclerosis diagnosis, patients must have evidence of demyelinating lesions that are separated in time and location. This evidence can be based on subjective symptoms or imaging evidence. This patient presents with evidence of lesions separated in space (a T10 spinal cord lesion, a lesion potentially affecting the medial longitudinal fasciculus, several corticospinal tract lesions as evidenced by diffuse hyperreflexia). Though the patient did not experience discrete symptomatic episodes separated by time, the presence of multiple lesions in discrete locations makes multiple sclerosis the most likely diagnosis (as the other deficits likely arose at different times). MRI of the brain typically shows white matter hyperintensities in the periventricular region, cortex, subcortical region, cerebellum, or spine. Oligoclonal bands of immunoglobu lins, indicating immune overactivation, can be found in the cerebrospinal fluid but are not necessary for diagnosis. Treatment includes corticosteroids for symptomatic management of acute flares and long-term disease-modifying treatments such as interferon or monoclonal antibodies.

questionStem: A 67-year-o ld woman is brought to the physician 3 hours after a 5-minute episode of visual loss in her left eye. She has not had any other symptoms. She has hypertens ion and stable angina pectoris. Medications include lisinopril and metoprolol. Her pulse is 72/min, and blood pressure is 150/92 mm Hg. Funduscopic exam ination shows no abnorma lities. A grade 3/6 holosystolic murmur is heard best at the apex. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnos is?
correctExplanation: Amaurosis fugax describes brief episodes of transient, unilateral vision loss and is indicative of retinal ischemia caused by either microembolization or inflammation of the ophthalmic artery. It often precedes the onset of central retinal artery occlusion , which is considered an ophthalmic stroke. In the absence of signs and symptoms of giant cell arteritis, such as fever, chills, weight loss, temporal headache and tenderness, or jaw claudication, amaurosis fugax is most suggestive of embolic retinal ischemia and should prompt an emergent evaluation for sources of emboli. The majority of emboli to the ophthalmic vasculature originate from the carotid arteries and cardiac valves. Evaluation should include prompt carotid duplex ultrasonography, as well as echocardiography. Treatment of carotid vascular or cardiac valvular disease can prevent central retinal arterial occlusion, which may cause irreversib le blindness.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Complete blood count (Choice A) and measurement of erythrocyte sedimentation rate (Choice B) are useful for the diagnosis of giant cell arteritis, which often presents with amaurosis fugax, thrombocytosis, and an increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate. However, this patient's lack of other symptoms renders carotid arterial disease, rather than giant cell arteritis, as the more likely cause of her amaurosis fugax. Visual field testing (Choice C) may be useful for the diagnosis of glaucoma or cortical vision loss. Delaying the search for embolic sources while pursuing other diagnostic tests puts the patient at risk for ischemic stroke and blindness. MRI of the brain (Choice D) may be useful for the diagnosis of optic neuritis. It is not useful for identifying the source of emboli that are causing this patient's amaurosis fugax. Vision loss secondary to optic neuritis typically lasts for several days or weeks, rather than minutes.

questionStem: An 11-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her mother because of a 2-day history of increasing weakness and a prickling sensation in her legs. She was previously healthy except for a mild flu-like illness during the past week. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 115/70 mm Hg. Examination of the lower extremities shows a muscle strength of 1 /5 and decreased sensation to pinprick. Achilles tendon and patellar reflexes are decreased . The remainder of the examination shows no abnorma lities. A lumbar puncture is performed. Analysis of cerebrospinal fluid shows a total protein concentration of 80 mg/dl and a leukocyte count of 4/mm3. In addition to close observat ion, oxygen therapy, and maintenance of fluids, which of the following is the most appropr iate pharmacotherapy?
correctExplanation: This patient most likely has Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS), leading to polyneuropathy, which is typically treated with immune globulins or plasma exchange. In GBS, a preceding infection (eg, Campylobacter jejuni, influenza-like illnesses) leads to autoimmune cross­ reactivity with the myelin of the nerve roots exiting the spinal cord. The ventral nerve roots, containing motor and sympathetic efferents, are most commonly involved, though the dorsal nerve root (controlling sensation) may also be affected. As such, patients typically present with acute symmetric muscle weakness with depressed or absent deep tendon reflexes (reflecting a lower motor neuron pattern of dysfunction) that begins in the lower extremities and may rapidly ascend to involve the upper extremities, bulbar muscles, or respiratory muscles. Autonomic dysfunction (eg, blood pressure fluctuations, cardiac irregularities) is common. Sensory deficits and pain can also occur (though these symptoms are typically mild compared to motor dysfunction). The diagnosis is confirmed by increased cerebrospinal fluid protein with normal cell counts on lumbar puncture, termed albuminocytologic dissociation, thought to reflect generalized inflammation. Management includes respiratory support and, for severe cases, plasma exchange or intravenous immunoglobulin therapy. Intravenous immunoglobulin therapy may work by neutralizing the cross-reactive antibodies that cause GBS.

However, these agents do not improve the symptoms of GBS. Anticonvulsants (Choice B) are utilized to treat seizure disorders but play no role in the treatment of GBS. questionStem: A 42-yea r-old woman with alcoholism has severe burning paresthesias of both feet and decreased vibratory sensation in both ankles 2 months after beginning treatme nt for active, cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis. At the time of diagnos is she was malnourished, and isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, vitami n B6, and folic acid were prescribed. The most likely cause of paresthesias of her feet and decreased sensation in her ankles is failure to take which of the following prescribed medications?
correctExplanation: Primary tuberculosis results from an initial exposure to Mycobacterium tuberculosis, leading to the development of hilar lymphadenopathy and a Ghon focus (Ghon complex), as in this case. In the primary infection, patients present with subacute fevers, weight loss, night sweats, cough, and malaise. Active tuberculosis is treated primarily with a combination of rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. lsoniazid binds vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) which may result in early excretion and inactivation of pyridoxine, and also inhibits pyridoxine phosphokinase, which is necessary to activate it. Pyridoxine deficiency then results, of which the primary symptoms are peripheral neuropathy or paresthesia. Therefore, all patients taking isoniazid concurrently take pyridoxine supplementation. Pyridoxine deficiency limits synthesis of histamine, hemoglobin, and neurotransmitters including epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine, serotonin, and y-aminobutyric acid (GABA). In addition to peripheral neuropathy, deficiency commonly presents with dermatitis, siderob lastic anemia, glossitis, and seizures.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Ethambuto l (Choice A) is used to treat mycobacterial infection. It neither contributes to nor prevents vitamin B6 deficiency. Its primary side effects include optic neuropathy, neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia. Folic acid (Choice B) is converted to tetrahydrofolic acid and is used as a coenzyme in the synthesis of nucleotides and nucleosides. Folate is contained in leafy vegetab les and absorbed in the jejunum. Folate deficiency is often seen in patients with malnutrition, alcohol use disorder, and patients taking anti-folate medications (eg, phenytoin, methotrexate). It is not caused by any of the medications used to treat tuberculosis. lsoniazid (Choice C) binds vitamin B6 and leads to deficiency if not adequate ly supplemented. questionStem: A 20-year-o ld college student comes to the physician for a follow-up examination 2 days after sustaining a head injury when he ran into another player while playing flag football. He did not lose consciousness but does not remember anything from the rest of the game. He was evaluated in the emergency department 1 hour after the injury; a CT scan of the head showed no abnorma lities and he was discharged. Today, he reports a mild, persistent headache that improves with acetaminophen. He has not had nausea, vomiting, or memory problems and was able to return to school today. Examination shows no abnormalities. He asks about playing i11 a flag football playoff game tomorrow. Which of the following is the most appropriate recomme ndation?

choices.A: No contact sports pending evaluation in 1 wee!<
choices.B: No contact sports pending an MRI of the brain
choices.C: No contact sports pending a lumbar puncture
choices.D: No contact sports for 1 year; schedule regular follow-up examinations

correctExplanation: Mild traumatic brain injury, also known as a concussion, commonly results in loss of consciousness, confusion, amnesia, headache, dizziness, nausea, or vomiting minutes after the injury. Symptoms that commonly develop within the following days include mood disturbances, photophonophobia, trouble concentrating, or insomnia. Focal neurologic symptoms, such as limb weakness or vision changes, indicate traumatic vascular injury. As such, all patients with suspected concussion should undergo a thorough neurologic examination, and a subset of at-risk patients should receive neuroimaging. All patients should be monitored closely for 24 hours for neurologic deterioration, which may indicate a developing intracranial hematoma. To prevent cumulative brain injury (eg, from a second concussion), patients with concussion should return to their usual activities in a graded fashion, beginning with the return to school or work. Each day, a more intense activity can be introduced (eg, first light aerobic exercise), culminating with contact sports after a week in uncomplicated and improving cases.

A lumbar puncture (Choice C) is not typically necessary for ruling out an intracranial hematoma in the setting of suspected concussion. Neuroimaging is sufficient. questionStem: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by paramedics after having a seizure at a dormitory party on campus. According to her boyfriend , who accompanied her, she had been drinking more water than usual and then became silent and began staring. He then witnessed her collapse to the floor and begin shaking for approximate ly 1 minute. On arrival, she is mute and unresponsive to questions. She appears restless and periodical ly grinds her teeth. Her temperature is 39.6°C (103.3°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 150/95 mm Hg. Physical examinat ion shows profuse diaphoresis and piloerection. Pupils are 5 mm bilaterally. The remainder of the examination shows no abnorma lities. Laboratory studies show: Prothrombin time Serum Na+ Urea nitrogen Creatinine ALT Creatine kinase 16 sec 114m Eq/L 40 mg/dL 2 mg/dL 90 U/L 1200 U/L The most likely diagnosis is intoxication with which of the following substances?
correctExplanation: 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MOMA), called ecstasy or "Molly," is a psychotherapeutic agent and drug of abuse. It is a stimulant and causes feelings of increased energy, euphoria, and disinhibition. Minor characteristic side effects include agitation, bruxism (grinding teeth), diaphoresis, and blurry vision. However, serious side effects also accompany ecstasy use. Autonomic instability (hypertension, tachycardia, and hyperthermia) can lead to life-threatening cardiovascular toxicity. This patient demonstrates another serious complication: hyponatremia secondary to increased water intake and secretion of anti-diuretic hormone. Severe hyponatremia may be accompanied by seizures, as seen in this case, as well as confusion, coma, or death. This is a particular risk in young women. Treatment includes rapid administration of hypertonic saline if recurrent seizure activity occurs, followed by gradual correction of sodium and management of autonomic instability.

questionStem: A 47-year-o ld man with a history of alcoho lism is brought to the emergency department by his fam ily because of confusion. He lives alone, and they found him disor iented 4 hours ago. An empty plastic container with a sweet odor was found in his apartment. He is oriented only to place. Cranial nerves, motor strength, and sensation are normal. Serum studies show a creatinine concentrat ion of 1.5 mg/dl, bicarbonate concentrat ion of 8 mEq/L, and an increased anion gap. Serum ketones test is negative. Urinalysis shows crystals. Exposure to which of the following is the most likely cause of these findings?
correctExplanation: Patients with ingestion of ethylene glycol may present similar ly to patients with alcohol intoxication, with central nervous system effects such as disorientation and altered menta l status. Ethylene glyco l is metabo lized by alcohol dehydrogenase to toxic metabo lites including glycolate, glyoxylate, and oxalate. These metabol ites are directly toxic to the kidneys through tubular damage as well as oxalate crysta l precipitation causing tubu le obstruction, resulting in acute kidney injury. Oxalate crystals are seen on urine microscopy. These metabolites also contribute to an anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Management of ethylene glyco l poisoning involves fomepizo le, an alcohol dehydrogenase inhibitor that prevents metabolization of ethy lene glyco l to its toxic metabo lites. For severe ingestions, hemodial ysis to remove ethy lene glyco l and its metabol ites may be necessary.

questionStem: A 77-year-old man with hyperte nsion comes to the physician for a routine follow-up examination. He feels well. His only medication is a diuretic. His blood pressure is 140/70 mm Hg. On neurologic examination, cranial nerves are intact. Muscle tone and strength are normal. Deep tendon reflexes are absent in the ankles but otherwise normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.A: Measureme nt of urine lead concentration

correctExplanation: A thorough neurologic examination should include evaluation of the cranial nerves, gait, coordination, movement, muscle strength and tone, light touch, pain and temperature sensation, deep tendon reflexes, and the plantar response (Babinski sign). Deep tendon reflexes can be checked over the biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, knee, and Achilles tendons using a reflex hammer. They are graded on a scale of Oto 4 where 0 is absent, 2 is normal, and 4 is clonus (continual contraction). Reflex strength should be compared on either side and within the same patient. The Achilles reflex test is particular ly useful for evaluating pathology of the S1 nerve root and differentiating upper from lower motor neuron dysfunction. However, bilaterally absent Achilles reflex is also a normal variation, the proportion of which increases with age. Thus, in this case, the absence of both Achilles reflexes does not require any additional management. Educational Objectives: A, B, C, and D. Measurement of urine lead concentration (Choice A) is appropriate when lead poisoning is suspected. Symptoms of lead poisoning occur within days or weeks of exposure and include distal motor neuropathy. While this does cause hyporeflexia, it would affect all the reflexes in the body, not just the Achilles. It would also cause other lower motor neuron symptoms such as muscle weakness, atrophy, and fasciculations, which this patient lacks. MRI of the lumbar spine (Choice B) would be beneficia l in evaluating hyporeflexia because of a spinal nerve or spinal cord lesion. Neither of these pathologies would present with bilaterally absent Achilles reflexes alone without other symptoms like back pain or muscle weakness. questionStem: An otherwise healthy 27-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of decreased libido and delayed ejaculation. He says that his symptoms are having a detrimental effect on his relationship. He has not had similar problems in the past. Four months ago, he was evaluated for low mood and loss of interest and productivity; his symptoms have been well controlled with sertraline since that time. He takes no other medications. Physical examinat ion shows no abnorma lities. Which of the following neurotrans mitters is most likely responsible for this patient's current symptoms?
correctExplanation: Increased serotonin likely explains this patient's sexual dysfunction. Sertraline is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) that increases synaptic serotonin activity and improves mood in patients with major depressive disorder. SSRls common ly cause sexual dysfunction within all three phases of sexual response (libido, sexual arousal, and orgasm). If the sexual dysfunction is persistent and distressing, management commonly involves lowering the SSRI dose, switching to an antidepressant with a lower risk for sexual dysfunction (eg, bupropion, mirtazapine), or adding bupropion or a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor such as sildenafil. Libido is typically enhanced by dopamine and gonadal hormones and may be inhibited by medications such as antipsychotics and SSRls. Arousal is promoted by acetylcholine, which leads to vasodilation of the helicine/vaginal arteries and consequent penile/clitora l tumescence. Medications with anticholinergic activity and SSRls inhibit arousal. Norepinephrine enhances orgasm (and ejaculation), and beta­ blockers and SSRls inhibit orgasm.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Acetylcholine (Choice A) mediates arousal via the vasodilation of the helicine or vaginal arteries. Medications with anticholinergic activity, which include paroxetine but not sertraline within the SSRI class, may inhibit arousal but would not likely affect libido or ejaculation. y-Aminobutyric acid (Choice B), or GABA, is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter. GABA is not known to be involved in sexual response. Dopamine (Choice C), which may be increased by methylphenidate, amphetamines, and cocaine, increases libido and may play a role in ejaculation. However, antidepressants do not affect dopamine signaling.

questionStem: A previous ly healt hy 27-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of a 2-week history of pain in his neck and left shou lder radiating through the latera l surface of his left arm to his thumb and index finger. Exam ination shows a decreased biceps reflex on the left. Muscle strength is 4/5 on extension of the left wrist. Sensat ion to light touch is decreased over the left thumb and index finger. The remainder of the examination, including neurologic examination, shows no abnormal ities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: C6 radiculopathy is the most likely diagnosis. The C6 dermatome is located on the lateral aspect of the forearm and extends to the latera l two digits of the hand. Injury to the C6 nerve roots will cause decreased sensation, pain, and/or paresthesia in these distributions along with motor dysfunction of elbow flexion and wrist extension. The C6 nerve root carries efferent information for the biceps reflex. Dermatomes and myotomes are components of the embryonic somite, a paired segment of paraxial mesoderm. When fully developed, the dermatome is an area of skin whose afferent fibers trave l within a single spinal nerve, and myotome is a group of muscles innervated by efferent fibers from a single spinal nerve. Radiculopathy refers to patho logy of a spinal nerve root and may be caused by spondylosis (degenerative changes of the spine), disc herniation, infection, tumor, demyelination, or infarction. Disc herniation and spondylosis are the most common causes and lead to compression of the nerve root as it exits the spinal cord. Sensory deficits, motor dysfunction, and pain typica lly occur in the dermatomal and myotomal distribution that corre lates to the affected nerve root.
incorrectExplanation: nd G. C4 radiculopathy (Choice A) would lead to sensory and motor dysfunction in the neck and shoulders around the acromioclavicu lar joint. Sensory and motor dysfunction in the distal upper extremity and an absent biceps reflex are more consistent with C6 radicu lopathy. C5 radiculopathy (Choice B) would lead to sensory and motor dysfunction in the latera l aspect of the shoulder and upper arm. C5 radiculopathy typica lly results in an absent biceps reflex, as the C5 nerve root carries afferent information for this reflex. However, C5 radiculopathy would not cause decreased sensation in the digits. - -- - -- - . - - - - - -- - -- .. - - - - -- - -- -- - - .. -- - - .. --- - -- ..

questionStem: A 72-year-old man comes to the physician because of a ?-day history of increas ingly severe pain around the waist. He says that it feels like a burning belt from the left midback to the umbilicus. He has a history of chron ic low back pain. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus treated with glyburide and asthma treated with beclome thasone and albuterol inhalers. He comple ted a 10-day course of corticostero ids for asthma 3 weeks ago. Examination shows numbness in the left T12 distribution. The remainder of the exam ination shows no abnor malities. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?
correctExplanation: This patient's history of diabetes and presenting signs and symptoms of burning pain in a dermatomal distribution are, in the absence of other findings, consistent with a diagnosis of diabetic radiculopathy. Formation of advanced glycation end products in chronic diabetics leads to microvascular ischemic damage to various tissues, including to the vasa nervorum. This mechanism underlies the pathogenesis of both diabetic polyneuropathy, as well as diabetic radiculopathy. Diabetic thoracic radiculopathy presents with unilatera l burning and electric-like pain extending from the back to the anterior abdomina l midline in a dermatomal distribution that may involve one or several spinal levels. Patients often experience numbness and muscular weakness of the affected nerve distribution. Most patients experience improvement in their symptoms over several months with conservative treatment.
incorrectExplanation: nd G. Ankylosing spondylitis (Choice A) is an autoimmune disorder affecting the axial joints, especial ly the intervertebral and sacroi liac joints. Patients present with slowly progressive, dull, lower back pain and stiffness that characteristically improves with activity. Patients usually present in the third decade of life and rarely experience burning pain. Atherosclerotic vascular disease (Choice B) may cause claudication, which presents with pain of the lower extremity that occurs in the setting of exercise and resolves with rest. Patients may experience coolness, pallor, hair loss, and poor wound healing of the affected limb. - - - - -- - .

questionStem: A 12-year-old girl with systemic lupus erythematosus is brought to the emergency department by her parents after they had difficulty awakening her this morning. She has needed constant stimulation to stay awake. Over the past 2 days, she has had a flu-like illness and vomiting. She has been unable to take her corticosteroid and antihypertensive medications. Her temperatu re is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 60/min, respirations are 40/min, and blood pressure is 180/130 mm Hg. She is obtunded but moves all extremities to painful stimuli. Funduscopic exam ination shows bilatera l papilledema with flame hemorrhages. Deep tendon reflexes are brisk and symmetric. Her erythrocyte sedimentation rate is 12 mm/h. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Hypertensive encephalopathy is a known complication of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and results from acute and severe increases in blood pressure. It may manifest with headache, vomiting, agitation, altered mental status, and seizure, and can progress to obtundation and coma. Visual symptoms may result from cortical hypertension or from hypertensive retinopathy, manifesting as papilledema and flame hemorrhages on fundoscopic examination. Treatment includes carefully lowering the blood pressure while avoiding excessively rapid drops, which can cause cerebral or cardiac ischemia. In genera l, a decrease in the mean arterial pressure of 25% within the first hour is appropriate, with gradual correction over the next day or more. Sodium nitroprusside is a potent vasodi lator and is a preferred agent because of its short half-life, allowing it to be titrated via intravenous infusion.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Brain neoplasm (Choice A) can cause altered mental status in a subacute or chronic time course. It would be less likely in this patient who is presenting with acute hypertensive encephalopathy. Cerebral vasculitis (Choice B) as a manifestation of SLE is rare. Cerebral vasculitis can present with neurologic deficits, headache, seizures, or coma. Hypertensive encephalopathy is more likely in this patient. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (Choice D) presents common ly in younger, overweight fema les taking vitamin A, oral contraceptives, or danazol. It is usually associated with a holocephalic headache and blurry vision.

questionStem: A previous ly healthy 4-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her parents because of a 3-day history of increased drowsiness. During this period, she also has been feeding poorly and "spitting up" after each feeding. She has not had fever. She was born at term following an uncompl icated pregnancy and delivery. On arrival, she is respons ive to tactile stimuli. She is at the 25th percenti le for length and weight and 90th percenti le for head circumference. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6 °F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 100/70 mm Hg. Examination shows a bulging anterior fontanel. There is a hyperpigmented macule with hair growth on the upper lumbar spine; her parents report that this finding was noted at birth. Which of the following is the most likely diagnos is?
correctExplanation: Chiari malformations are rare congenita l malformations that typical ly present in infancy with feeding and breathing problems, spina bifida (classically manifesting as myelomeningocele), and obstructive hydrocephalus (presenting as large head circumference and bulging anterior fontane l in this patient) as a result of the downward displacement of the cerebellar vermis and tonsils. This patient's hyperpigmented macule with hair growth on the upper lumbar spine likely represents spina bifida occulta (a small defect in the vertebrae). Some patients also demonstrate eye movement abnormalities. Some Chiari malformations present in adolescence with bilateral cranial nerve palsies, weakness, and cerebellar dysfunction as a result of the downward displacement of the cerebel lar tonsils and consequent brainstem compression. Imaging typically demonstrates downward displacement of the cerebe llar vermis and tonsils, along with ventriculomegaly from hydrocephalus. Treatment involves surgical intervention for neural tube defects, shunting for hydrocephalus, and medical management of feeding and respiratory difficulties.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Bacterial meningitis (Choice A) typica lly presents with fever and signs of meningeal irritation (nausea, irritability, confusion, anorexia, headache, and nuchal rigidity). Spina bifida occulta is not associated with acute bacterial meningitis. Hydrocephalus may result from bacterial meningitis. Idiopathic increased intracrania l pressure (Choice C) would present with symptoms of increased intracranial pressure (nausea, vomiting, positional headache) without hydrocephalus or other central nervous system pathology. Spina bifida occulta would be atypical. - - - - - - - - - - - - - -- - - - - - .

questionStem: A 13-year-old girl is brought to the physician because of headac hes accompanied by nausea and vomiting over the past 2 weeks; they are located behind the left eye and improve after sleep. The headaches started during final examinat ions, and she now is missing 2 to 3 days of school weekly because of the pain. Her temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 90/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 95/60 mm Hg. Examination shows no abnorma lities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Migraine is a common condition that presents with recurrent primary headaches. Migraine headaches are typically severe, unilateral, throbbing, and associated with nausea, vomiting, photophobia, and phonophobia. The pain is usually located behind or adjacent to the eye. Some patients additiona lly experience an aura before or during the headache, which may present with vision loss followed by the perception of scintillating shapes or lines or paresthesia. Migraine triggers include stress, menstruation, weather changes, fasting, and alcoholic beverages. Sleep may improve migraines. Migraines are postulated to arise from deficient serotonin inhibition of descending pain pathways. Acute migraine treatment includes triptans and/or nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). For patients with disabling or frequent migraines, prophylactic treatment is also recommended and includes ~-adrenergic blockers, antidepressants such as tricyclic antidepressants and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors, and anticonvulsants.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Brain tumor (Choice A) may cause generalized headaches associated with vomiting that typically occur while patients are lying supine as a result of increased intracranial pressure and may be accompanied by papilledema and blurred vision. This patient's headache improved in the supine position. Cluster headaches (Choice B) are primary headaches that typically present with short-lived, unilateral, severe pain in the orbital, supraorbital, or temporal region of the head and are accompanied by ipsilateral autonomic symptoms (eg, miosis, ptosis, lacrimation, nasal congestion). This patient did not demonstrate autonomic symptoms. Sinusitis (Choice D) may be associated with bilateral, pressure-like, periorbital headaches and nasal congestion. Headaches are not typically associated with nausea, vomiting, photophobia, or phonophobia. This patient's unilatera l headaches that started during a stressful period are more consistent with migraine.

questionStem: Over the past year, a 72-year-old man has had progressive aching in his lower extremities when he walks in the shopp ing mall. Initial ly, the pain began after 15 minutes of walking and resolved after he stopped; now, it starts after 5 or 10 minutes of walking, and it occas ionally occurs when he stands up after sleeping all night. The pain radiates from his buttocks to his feet. He desc ribes it as a "terrib le" pain. He has mild chronic obstructive pulmonary disease but cont inues to smoke one pack of cigarettes daily. He has cervical arthritis and often has neck and arm pain. Exam ination shows decreased breath sounds bilatera lly. Strength and sensation are normal in the extremities. correctExplanation: Lumbar spinal stenosis refers to the narrowing of the lumbar spinal canal, which results in compression of the lumbar nerve roots or spinal cord. Patients may present with symptoms of radicu lopathy, including back pain that radiates to the buttocks and legs, leg numbness, paresthesia, or weakness. Hip extension increases pressure on the nerve roots, while flexion of the hips relieves pressure. Consequently, patients may demonstrate neurogenic claudication, in which extension of the hips (eg, standing or walking) leads to symptoms. The most common cause of lumbar spinal stenosis is degenerative joint disease and osteophytosis, which often occurs with age. The diagnosis is confirmed by MRI. Treatment involves nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, physical therapy, and surgery.

His pain is relieved by stretching. There is no history of trauma. He is otherwise healthy except for occasional dysuria. questionStem: A 67-year-o ld woman is brought to the emergency depart ment 1 hour after a 25-m inute episode of right facia l droop, weakness of the right arm and hand, and an inability to talk. She has hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, coronary artery disease, chron ic atrial fibr illation, and gout. Her medications include metoprolol, fosinopril, glyburide, and allopurinol. correctExplanation: Transient ischemic attack is defined as a transient episode of neurologic dysfunction caused by focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia without evidence of infarction. This patient has multiple risk factors for ischemic stroke including hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, atherosclerotic disease, and atrial fibrillation. An embolic ischemic stroke involves an event in which a clot breaks off and travels to the brain, occluding blood flow at a cerebral artery. Emboli can come from proximal vessels, such as the internal carotid artery, or from an atrial thrombus. This patient has an atrial thrombus, which can embolize and cause an ischemic stroke. After a transient ischemic attack, measures for prevention of an ischemic stroke should be enacted. Many causes of syncope are identifiable based on the history, and the patient's age and comorbidities. For example, vasovagal syncope is associated with a brief prodrome of lightheadedness, nausea, and diaphoresis, often in association with a fear-inducing event (eg, a patient loses consciousness when seeing a needle or blood). It occurs due to a sudden increase in vagal tone, leading to vasodilation and bradycardia (resulting in low cardiac output). In this case, the patient experienced a brief prodrome of pallor and diaphoresis, followed by LOC, in the setting of advanced age and a cardiac comorbidity. His age and cardiac history increase the likelihood of cardiogenic syncope (eg, a transient non-perfusing arrhythmia such as ventricu lar tachycardia); thus, investigation shou ld occur to determine the cause and prevent future episodes. Syncope is often accompanied by micturition, tongue biting, jerking, or twitching - these events are not exclusive ly associated with seizures. Syncope is generally not accompanied by a postictal period; patients usually return to their menta l base line within minutes of the event.

questionStem: A 47-yea r-old woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of gradual hearing loss in the left ear. She also has had difficulty maintaining her balance over the past 3 months. Six months ago, she had an episode of nephrolithiasis complicated by a severe urinary tract infection requiring intravenous antibiotic therapy. Examination shows a decrease of the left nasolab ial fold and a slight perioral droop when she smiles. The forehead movements are intact bilaterally. Her gait is normal, but she has difficulty with tandem walking. Audiomet ry shows moderate high-frequency hearing loss on the left with impaired speech discrimination. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: This patient most likely has an acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) compressing the vestibulocochlear nerve and the upper motor neurons that synapse on the facial nerve. Acoustic neuromas are benign tumors consisting of Schwann cells that arise from the vestibu locochlear nerve (cranial nerve VIII). Lesions of the vestibulocochlear nerve typically disrupt ipsilateral hearing and the sensation of head and body position, which leads to difficulty with balance and tandem (heel-to-toe) gait as in this patient. Mass effect from progressive ly enlarging acoustic neuromas can compress the neighboring facial nerve or the upper motor neurons synapsing on the facial nerve, leading to a flattened nasolabial fold and perioral droop. If the upper motor neurons are affected, the forehead is spared, as the facial nerve nucleus that controls forehead musculature is dually innervated by upper motor neurons from bilateral precentral gyri. Because of this, the patient would be expected to symmetrically raise her eyebrows. Alternatively, lesions involving the lower motor neurons of facial expression (eg, facial nerve inflammation in Bell palsy) affect the forehead and lower face together. Depending on patient age, tumor size, and symptom burden, acoustic neuromas can be managed with observation, radiation, or surgery.

correctExplanation: This patient's findings of headache and bitemporal hemianopsia are consistent with a diagnosis of pituitary adenoma. Benign adenomas are the most common neoplasms identified in the pituitary gland, and may secrete hormones, such as prolactin or growth hormone, causing symptoms of hyperpituitarism. More common ly, pituitary mass lesions do not cause hyperpituitarism but instead cause compression of normal pituitary neurons, leading to hypopituitarism and dysfunction of multiple endocrine axes. The pituitary gland rests in the bony sella turcica, just inferior to the optic chiasm. Retinal gang lion cell fibers from the nasal retina, which supply the temporal visual fields, decussate at the chiasm, and are vulnerable to compression by pituitary mass lesions. Since the decussating nasal retinal fibers carry information from the temporal visual fields, the resultant visual field deficit is most commonly a bitemporal hemianopsia, a finding suggestive of a pituitary mass.

Pituitary adenoma is a more likely diagnosis in a previous ly healthy adult. Medulloblastoma (Choice C) is a common malignancy of the brain in children. questionStem: A 25-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of worsening excess ive daytime sleepiness, even during important events such as meetings at work. She says she has trouble sustain ing her attention and that her symptoms are beginning to impair her work productivity. She also reports occasional episodes in which her muscles go limp and she falls sudden ly. She has injured herself during two of these episodes. She is 163 cm (5 ft 4 in) tall and weighs 59 kg (130 lb); BMI is 22 kg/m2. Her pulse is 85/min, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 120/76 mm Hg. Physical examinat ion shows no abnorma lities. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?
correctExplanation: Narcolepsy is a chronic sleep disorder characterized by daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, hypnagogic hallucinations, and sleep paralysis that responds to modafinil therapy. Narcolepsy arises from deficient production of orexins in the hypothalamus, which may result from genetic or autoimmune causes. Orexins typica lly induce the secretion of monoamines such as norepinephrine throughout the brain to promote wakefulness. As a result, patients suddenly and inappropriate ly transition into sleep during the day. Further, rapid-eye movement (REM) sleep features (eg, cataplexy, hypnagogic hallucinations, sleep paralysis) occur during wakefulness. Cataplexy refers to a sudden loss of muscle tone and usually occurs in response to positive emotion. The clinical diagnosis should be confirmed by a polysomnography (to confirm the rapid transition into REM sleep and rule out other causes of daytime sleepiness) and a multiple sleep latency test (to confirm decreased sleep latency). Treatment includes a regular sleep schedule, avoidance of daytime naps, and, in patients with severe daytime sleepiness, modafinil. Modafinil has an unclear mechanism of action that involves increasing orexin and monoamine availability.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Weight loss program (Choice A), continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) (Choice B), and uvulopalatopharyngoplasty (Choice F) all target obstructive sleep apnea. Obstructive sleep apnea features repetitive obstruction of the pharyngeal airway during sleep and typica lly occurs in older, male patients with obesity as a result of a combination of structura l, vascular, and neuromuscular factors. Patients become hypoxemic several times nightly and experience fragmented sleep, leading to daytime sleepiness. REM sleep phenomena during wakefulness is instead consistent with narco lepsy. In patients with suspected narcolepsy, comorbid obstructive slee a nea should be ruled out with ol somno ra h .

questionStem: A 68-year-o ld woman comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of a spinning sensation. She reports feeling as though the room is spinning particular ly when she tries to turn over in bed; the feeling usually resolves within 1 minute. She has no vomiting with an episode but does feel a little queasy. Examination shows normal hearing . Ocular movemen ts are full when the patient is sitting, but when her head is allowed to hang off the examination table, she develops a coarse, rotatory nystagmus beating to one side. The remainder of the exam ination shows no abnorma lities. The most likely cause of this patient's condition is an abnormality at which of the following sites?
correctExplanation: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is a common cause of vertigo that occurs as a result of a calcium carbonate particle (otoconium) that gets displaced from the otolith organs into the adjacent semicircu lar canals. The otolith organs and semicircu lar canals are located in the inner ear and sense movement of the head. Normally, otoconia are contained within the matrix of the otolith organs, adding weight to the organs so that the organs shift in position when head position changes. When otoconia become dislodged, they cause abnormal movement of the endolymph within the semicircular canals and the subsequent sensation of head movement. Consequently, patients present with minutes-long, abrupt episodes of vertigo that may be accompanied by nausea, which resolve when holding still. The cochlear apparatus is intact, resulting in norma l hearing. Symptom resolution with particle repositioning maneuvers such as the Epley maneuver serves to both diagnose and treat BPPV. Vertigo is the sensation that the surroundings are moving and is associated with lesions of the peripheral or central vestibular system. Peripheral vertigo is typically short- lived and sudden in onset, whereas central vertigo is insidious in onset and may cause constant and sustained vertigo. Peripheral causes of vertigo such as BPPV may also present with uni- or multidirectional nystagmus and may decrease as patients focus their gaze, while central causes of vertigo such as brainstem tumors or strokes typically lead to purely unidirectional nystagmus that does not improve with primary gaze.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Lesions of the auditory cortex (Choice A), located in the temporal lobe, result in impairment of the conscious perception of auditory sensations. The vestibular cortices are instead distributed across the parietal and temporal cortices. A brain stem (Choice B) mass of the cerebellopontine angle (eg, acoustic neuroma, meningioma, glioma) typically affects the vestibulocochlear nerve and may also affect other cranial nerves (eg, trigeminal, abducens, facial nerves). questionStem: A 10-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents after the Thanksgiving holiday break because of a 4-day history of rapid, irregular involuntary movements of her face, trunk, and extremities. Her parents say that during this period, she has been anxious and irritable and has had headaches. She seems to be worry ing obsessive ly about things that formerly would not have worried her. She has no history of serious illness except for migratory joint pain that occurred in the early fall. Examination shows restless-appearing, genera lized involuntary movements of the face, trunk, and extremities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

choices.A: Autoimmune disorder of the basal ganglia

correctExplanation: This patient likely has Sydenham chorea, which is a manifestation of an autoimmune disorder of the basal ganglia. The combination of choreiform movements and migratory joint pain suggest a diagnosis of rheumatic fever, a complication of Streptococcus pyogenes (group A) infection. Though arthritis is typically an early manifestation of acute rheumatic fever, Sydenham chorea is a latent manifestation and may occur months after the initial streptococcal infection. In acute rheumatic fever, streptococca l infection causes immune cross-reactivity with neurona l and cardiac cell membrane proteins and the deposition of immune complexes in the joints and soft tissues. The binding of antibodies to basal ganglia neurons results in choreiform movements (involuntary, random, irregular movements) of the face, trunk, and extremities that may be more prominent on one side of the body. Neuropsychiatric symptoms such as emotional !ability and obsessive-compulsive disorder (a disorder associated with basal ganglia pathology) may also occur. Sydenham chorea may occur as an isolated manifestation of acute rheumatic fever or in conjunction with arthritis, carditis, erythema marginatum, and/or subcutaneous nodules. As such, patients with Sydenham chorea should receive an echocardiography to evaluate for carditis. The treatment of acute rheumatic fever involves nonsteroida l anti-inf lammatory drugs and penicillin to ensure the eradication of Streptococcus pyogenes (group A). Sydenham chorea is typical ly self-limited, but severe and impairing neuropsychiatric symptoms may be managed with antipsychotic or anticonvulsant medication.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Conversion disorder (Choice B), or functional neurologic disorder, involves acute neurologic symptoms such as sensory or motor dysfunction that are not fully explained by objective findings on physical examination or imaging. This patient's symptoms and physical examination findings are instead consistent with a known disease.

questionStem: A 32-year-o ld woman with breast cancer metastatic to bone is brought to the emergency department because of a 12-hour history of severe pelvic pain and numbness. She has not urinated for more than 24 hours. Her only medication is hydrocodo ne. On arrival, her temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 152/70 mm Hg. Rectal examination shows decreased rectal sphincter tone. Muscle strength is 4/5 in the lower extremities. Sensation to light touch is decreased in a saddle distribution. Abdomina l examination shows suprapubic fullness. Placement of a urinary catheter yields 800 ml of clear yellow urine and resolves the pelvic pain but not the numbness. An MRI of the spine shows a tumor pushing into the L4-S 1 intrathecal space. Which of the following is the most appropr iate immediate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Cauda equina syndrome occurs because of compression of the spinal nerve roots comprising the cauda equina. Often, such compression occurs as a result of malignancy, trauma (eg, compression fractures with fragment retropulsion), disc herniation, spinal stenosis, spinal epidural abscess, or spinal epidura l or subdural hematoma. Symptoms include lower extremity numbness, weakness, paralysis, hyporeflexia, perinea! anesthesia, fecal incontinence with poor rectal tone, and overflow incontinence marked by inability to void and urinary retention. Emergent MRI of the lumbosacral spine is indicated to investigate the cause of cauda equina syndrome, and to determine the necessity of surgical decompression. Initial treatment for patients with epidural spinal cord compression and neurologic deficits include symptomatic treatment, pain control, and glucocorticoid therapy prior to operative therapy. High-dose glucocorticoid therapy (eg, dexamethasone) is helpful as a bridge to definitive therapy, can help control pain, and may transient ly improve neurologic function secondary to decreasing edema at the site of cord compression.

In a patient who takes hydrocodone and is opiate-tolerant, pain control will likely require opioid analgesics. Intravenous or intrathecal administration of chemotherapy (Choices C and D) or radiation therapy (Choice E) may all be helpful for definitive treatment of the tumor, but glucocorticoids are the next immediate step in management. Radiation therapy can help with expeditious local control of spinal metastases. Chemotherapy can be helpful for tumors causing cauda equina, however, systemic chemotherapy may take days to weeks to take effect. questionStem: A 42-year-o ld woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband after he found her in a confused state when he returned home from a 3-day fishing trip. She has a long-standing relapsing psychiatric condition controlled with lithium carbonate, haloperidol, and clonazepam. She does not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. She appears drowsy. Her temperature is 37.5°C (99.5°F), pulse is 85/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 140/90 mm Hg. The pupils are 2 mm and reactive. There is a coarse tremor of the upper extrem ities. Deep tendon reflexes are increased throughout. She responds only to vigorous stimulation. On mental status examinat ion, her speech is slow and slurred. She appears perplexed and sleepy and does not respond to questions. Laboratory studies show: Leukocyte count 14,000/mm3 Serum Urea nitrogen Creatinine Lithium 60 mg/dL 2.5 mg/dL 3.5 mEq/dL (therapeutic range=0.6-1.2) In addition to discont inuing lithium carbonate, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: The patient presents with signs and symptoms of lithium toxicity including confusion, neuromuscular excitabi lity, coarse tremors, and myoclonic jerks. Severe lithium toxicity can cause seizures, status epilepticus, and encepha lopathy. Lithium is also associated with kidney toxicity and end-stage kidney disease. Lithium is filtered in the glomeru lus and is reabsorbed in the proximal tubules. Increased lithium reabsorption can occur in states of volume depletion and decreased lithium clearance can occur in kidney impairment. Management of lithium toxicity includes intravenous fluid resuscitation to maximize lithium clearance. Hemodialysis may be necessary in patients with severe lithium toxicity, seizures, altered mental status, or end-stage kidney disease resulting in impaired ability to excrete lithium.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Observation only (Choice A) would be inappropriate in this patient with severe lithium toxicity. Lithium is primarily excreted in the urine, which would be impaired in this patient with acute kidney injury. Therefore, in this case, lithium should be cleared by hemodialysis.

questionStem: A previous ly healt hy 62-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of intermittent drooping of his left eyelid and episodes of double vision. Neurologic examinat ion shows bilatera l ptosis, more prominent on the left. There is weakness of left eye abduction and adduction and weakness of right eye abduction. Pupillary reflexes are normal. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. This patient is at greatest risk for which of the following?
correctExplanation: This patient's presenting findings of intermittent ptosis, diplopia, and reduction of extraocular movements are suggestive of myasthenia gravis. Myasthenia gravis is a B lymphocyte-driven autoimmune disorder characterized by the formation of inhibitory anti-acetylcholine receptor autoantibodies. Patients typically experience muscular weakness and fatigue that worsens toward the end of the day, as well as ocular symptoms of drooping eyelids and diplopia. Many patients present with ocular findings and later develop generalized symptoms involving the proximal muscles. In severe exacerbations (myasthenic crises), patients may deve lop weakness of the muscles of the throat, diaphragm, and chest wall, leading to dysphagia and acute respiratory failure. Myasthenia gravis is diagnosed with the detection of serum autoantibodies. A chest x-ray is useful for detecting the presence of thymoma, which frequently produces myasthenia gravis as a paraneoplastic phenomenon. Some patients experience resolution of symptoms after surgical resection of a thymoma, although most patients require treatment with corticosteroids and acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (eg, pyridostigmine). Myasthenic crisis is treated with intravenous immune globulin, plasmapheresis, intubation, and mechanical ventilation.

While colon cancer may produce paraneoplastic findings, such as the Leser-Trelat sign, characterized by the sudden appearance of numerous seborrheic keratosis on the back and trunk, it does not typically cause myasthenia gravis. Lymphoma (Choice B) may occur in the orbit, typically involving the conjunctiva or the orbital adnexal tissues such as the lacrimal gland, extraocular muscles, and eyelids. Patients typica lly present with unilateral proptosis and may present with ptosis or diplopia. However, these symptoms would be progressive and unremitting, rather than intermittent. questionStem: Over the past 3 months, a 60-year-o ld woman has had 2-minute episodes characterized by a rising sensation in the abdomen followed by loss of awareness. During an episode, she stares, makes chewing movements, and makes fumb ling moveme nts with her hands; afterwards, she is confused for a few minutes. Visual fields are shown. Neurologic examination shows no other abnormalities. The most likely diagnosis is a lesion at which of the following locations?
correctExplanation: This patient's visual fields demonstrate a left superior field quadrantanopia. In conjunction with her symptoms of seizures, characterized by staring, chewing movements, automatisms of the hands, and postictal confusion, a left superior field quadrantanopia raises concern for a lesion of the right tempora l lobe, such as an astrocytoma. After decussating at the optic chiasm, retinal gang lion cell axons carrying information from the left visual field traverse the optic radiations and synapse at the lateral geniculate nucleus. This patient's visual fields demonstrate a left superior field quadrantanopia. In conjunction with her symptoms of seizures, characterized by staring, chewing movements, automatisms of the hands, and postictal confusion, a left superior field quadrantanopia raises concern for a lesion of the right tempora l lobe, such as an astrocytoma. After decussating at the optic chiasm, retinal ganglion cell axons carrying information from the left visual field traverse the optic radiations and synapse at the lateral geniculate nucleus. Neurons from the lateral geniculate nucleus travel to the primary visual cortex via the optic radiations, which divide into superior and inferior divisions. The right superior division travels through the right parietal lobe and carries information from the right inferior visual fields. In contrast, the right inferior division travels through the right temporal lobe by looping around the inferior horn of the lateral ventricle, forming the Meyer loop, and carries information from the right superior visua l fields. Lesions of the tempora l lobe that interrupt the Meyer loop produce a characteristic contralatera l superior quadrantanopia, a visua l defect described as a wedge-shaped loss of vision.
