Lesions affecting the frontal eye fields can produce an ipsilateral conjugate gaze preference but do not produce visua l field deficits. The occipital lobe (Choice B) is the location of the primary visual cortex. Lesions of the occipital lobe produce homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing. The optic nerve (Choice C) carries all the visual information from the retina of its respective eye. A lesion of the optic nerve, such as in the setting of glioma, demye linating optic neuritis, or trauma, produces a complete visual field defect of one eye. The parietal lobe (Choice D) contains the superior division of the optic radiation, which carries information from the inferior visua l fields. A unilateral lesion of the parietal lobe may produce a contralateral inferior visual field quadrantanopia. Educational Objective: Temporal lobe lesions that interrupt the Meyer loop of the inferior division of the optic radiation produce a characteristic contralateral superior visua l field quadrantanopia. Superior visual field quadrantanopia in conjunction with symptoms of seizures should raise suspicion for a mass of the tempora l lobe, such as an astrocytoma.

questionStem: A previous ly healthy 57-year-o ld man comes for a follow-up examination because of progress ive weakness of his arms and legs. Six months ago, examination showed no abnorma lities except for 4/5 muscle strength in all extrem ities. Current examinat ion shows fascicu lations in the hands and right lower extremity and pseudobu lbar palsy. Sensat ion is normal and cranial nerves are intact. He is oriented, and affect is appropriate. An MRI of the brain shows no abnorma lities. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of this patient's disease?

choices.D: Neoplastic infiltration of the central nervous system
choices.F: Neuronal loss in the substantia nigra

correctExplanation: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder arising in midlife that affects both lower motor neurons arising from the anterior horn and upper motor neurons of the lateral corticospinal tract within the brain and spinal cord. Neurons degenerate because of an unknown etiology that may involve RNA processing and/or excitotoxicity, and gliosis results. Patient presentations are variable, though typically feature a combination of upper motor neuron (eg, increased muscle tone, hyperreflexia, Babinski sign) and lower motor neuron findings (eg, decreased muscle tone, hyporeflexia, early muscle atrophy) in an asymmetric distribution that may include the bulbar muscles. Some patients may experience cognitive or behavioral changes, though other patients are cognitively normal. The diagnosis is primarily clinical but may be supported by electromyographic findings of acute and chronic denervation and reinnervation. MRI of the brain and spine should be performed to rule out other diseases. Treatment should include riluzole, which may modestly improve survival but does not cure the disease.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Amyloid deposition (Choice A) occurs in Alzheimer disease. Alzheimer disease may feature apraxia (potentially related to parietal cortex damage) but does not typically lead to upper neuron or lower motor neuron dysfunction. Demyelination (Choice B) occurs in acute conditions such as pontine myelinolysis and chronic autoimmune disorders such as multiple sclerosis. Demyelination can affect the white matter of the corticospinal tract but would not affect the anterior horns (gray matter). Neoplastic infiltration of the central nervous system (Choice D) may lead to localized upper motor neuron dysfunction because of mass effect. However, generalized dysfunction in both an upper and lower motor neuron pattern is more consistent with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.

questionStem: A 62-year-o ld man is brought to the physician by his wife because of a 3-year history of progressive forgetfulness. He has difficulty remembering names, especia lly of people he has recently met. He retired from his profession as a retail clerk 12 weeks ago because he had been forgetting the names of customers and new products and could no longer effectively perform his job. He also has had progressive difficulty with activities of daily living; his wife now chooses his clothes for him. He has no history o1f head trauma. He has no history of serious illness and takes no medications. He does not drink alcohol or use illicit drugs. Physical examination shows no abnorma lities. On mental status examination, he has an indifferent mood and affect. He is oriented to person, place, and time but takes a few minutes before he correctly names the date. His Mini-Menta l State Examination score is 22/30. There is no evidence of auditory or visua l hallucinations. Results of laboratory studies are within the reference ranges. Administration of a drug from which of the following classes is most appropriate for this patient?
correctExplanation: Alzheimer dementia (AD) results from decreased cholinergic signaling and is treated with acetylcho linesterase inhibitors. Cholinergic neurons-which primarily originate from the locus coeruleus and basal forebrain and project widely to areas including the cortex­ mediate attention, learning, and memory. AD is the most prevalent dementia, presenting with progressive cognitive decline that begins with short-term memory impairment and decline in visuospatial abilities and progresses to apraxia, language abnormalities, and dysexecutive syndrome (resulting in the inability to pick out clothes in this patient). The disease culminates in behaviora l and personality changes that prevent the patient from performing basic activities of daily living, such as bathing. Acetylcholinesterase normally hydrolyzes acetylcholine in synaptic clefts. Donepezil and other cholinesterase inhibitors non-competitively and reversibly inhibit acetylcholinesterase activity and thereby increase the amount of synaptic acetylcholine available for neurotransmission. Though donepezil may slow the rate of cognitive decline and modestly improve functiona lity, donepezil and the other cholinesterase inhibitors are not curative.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Dopamine agonists (Choice B) increase dopamine signaling and therefore relieve parkinsonism. This patient does not demonstrate motor findings typical of Parkinson disease such as tremor, bradykinesia, or postural instability. NMDA receptor agonists (Choice C), such as endogenous glutamate, mediate activity-dependent synaptic changes of learning and memory. Howeve r, NMDA agonism is not a known drug mechanism because of the risk for excitotoxicity.

questionStem: A 32-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance 20 minutes after he was found by a janito r on the floor of a restroom at a bus station. At the scene, he was having continuous, genera lized tonic-clon ic seizures. An endotracheal tube was placed, and supplementa l oxygen was administered. On arrival to the emergency department, he is flushed and diaphoret ic. There are no external signs of trauma. His temperatu re is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 15/min, and blood pressure is 140/70 mm Hg. The pupils are 4 mm and reactive to light. Examination shows tonic stiffening of the trunk and synchronous clonic jerking of the extrem ities. In addition to intravenous administration of dextrose, which of the following is the most appropriate next step in treatme nt?
correctExplanation: Status epilepticus is defined as continuous epileptic activity for at least five minutes, or at least two discrete seizures with incomp lete interval recovery of consciousness. Status epilepticus is a neurologic emergency that portends increased morbidity and requires prompt evaluation and treatment. The first-line treatment for convulsive status epilepticus involves benzodiazepines (eg, lorazepam, midazolam, or diazepam), which have been shown to control seizures rapidly. Benzodiazepines bind the GABAA receptor, a chloride channel, and increase the frequency of its opening. y-Aminobutyric acid (GABA) is an inhibitory neurotransmitter that counterbalances neuronal excitation, making benzodiazepines an effective treatment for seizure cessation.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Fosphenytoin (Choice A) blocks sodium channels and is typically a second-line choice in the treatment of status epilepticus. Benzodiazepines are the first-line treatment of convulsive status epilepticus. Naloxone (Choice C) is an opioid receptor antagonist used in the treatment of opiate or opioid overdoses, which classica lly present with bradypnea and pinpoint pupils. Naloxone has also been used to treat clonidine overdose. Phenobarbital (Choice D) can be effective for controlling seizures, however it is not the first-line pharmacotherapy as a result of slow administration and adverse effects of prolonged sedation and hypotension. Valproic acid (Choice E) increases sodium channel inactivation and increases GABA concentration. It is typically second- line in the treatment of status epilepticus.

questionStem: A previous ly healthy 37-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department because of a 10-day history of increasingly severe headaches. The pain has been unremitt ing for the past 18 hours; he describes it as severe and pounding. His pulse is 70/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 142/90 mm Hg. Examination of the face and neck shows mild swelling and a dusky reddish-purple skin color with venous distention over the head and neck; the skin color below the neck is normal. Examinat ion of the optic fundi shows papilledema. Neurologic examinat ion shows no focal findings. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's increased intracrania l pressure?

choices.C: Obstruct ion of cerebrospina l fluid flow
choices.D: Obstruction of venous return to the heart

correctExplanation: Obstruction of venous return to the heart through the superior vena cava (SVC) leads to superior vena cava syndrome, which presents with facial swelling, headaches, and occasional ly altered mental status or respiratory distress. Superior vena cava syndrome is most common ly caused by extrinsic compression of the SVC by an intrathoracic malignancy, such as lung cancer or lymphoma. Physical examination typically shows facial plethora, venous distension over the head and neck, and papilledema, as in this patient. While a chest x-ray may be abnormal, CT venography is typically diagnostic. Stent placement and radiation therapy are used to treat symptoms, but superior vena cava syndrome is classically associated with a poor prognosis.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Dilation of cerebral arteries (Choice A) is associated with the development of migraine headaches, which present with unilateral, pounding-type headaches that are associated with photophobia and phonophobia. They typically last for less than 48 to 72 hours and may have a preceding aura. They do not cause facial plethora and venous distension. An intracrania l mass lesion (Choice B) classically presents with focal neurologic deficits, such as hemiplegia, altered mental status, and signs of increased intracranial pressure, such as headache and nausea. Physical examination may demonstrate papilledema. However, it would not be expected to cause discoloration of the face or venous distension of the head and neck. Obstruction of cerebrospinal fluid flow (Choice C) and overproduction of cerebrospinal fluid (Choice E) can both lead to hydrocephalus. Hydrocephalus commonly presents with headache, altered mental status or behavior, and nausea or vomiting because of increased intracranial pressure. While papilledema may be present, venous distension would not be.

questionStem: Five days after a left hemicolectomy for colon cancer, a 62-year-old man is transferred to the intensive care unit because of temperatures to 40.6°C (105°F), lethargy, diaphores is, and labile blood pressure for 3 hours. His postoperative course had been complicated by temperatures to 37.8°C (100°F) and nocturnal agitation since day 2; he has required haloperidol therapy (2 mg nightly). He has a history of bipolar disorde r. Medications include morphine by patient-controlled analgesia pump, lithium carbonate, and clonazepam. He is lying expression less in a pool of sweat and is drooling. His temperature is 40.6°C (105°F), pulse is 140/min, and blood pressure is 180/100 mm Hg. Examination shows wet skin and dry mucosa. There is a herpetic lesion on his lower lip. The neck is supple and the intraveno us catheter insertion site is nontender with no erythema. Bowel sounds are hyperactive; there is no organomega ly. The wound is clean and dry with no erythema. Neurologic examination shows a masked facies and a marked intention tremor. Deep tendon reflexes are hyperactive and symmetric. Babinski sign is absent. Laboratory studies show: Hemoglob in Leukocyte count Segmented neutrophils Bands Lymphocytes Monocytes Serum Urea nitrogen Creatinine Creatine kinase 15 g/dL 20,000/mm 3 80% 5% 10% 5% 38 mg/dL 1.6 mg/dL 1000 U/L Urinalys is and an x-ray of the chest show no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is most likely in this patient who has received high-potency antipsychotic medication. NMS is a life-threatening condition associated with the antagonism of dopamine that presents with altered mental status, muscle rigidity or tremor, hyperthermia, and autonomic dysfunction. Common causative agents are antipsychotics (especia lly high-potency antipsychotics r ~, ~ ~ r, Previous Next Score Report Lab Values Calculator Help Pause .... https://t.me/USMLENBME2CK Exam Section: Item 38 of 50 National Board of Medical Examiners ■ Mark Clinical Neurology Self-Assessment Correct Answer: E. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is most likely in this patient who has received high-potency antipsychotic medication. NMS is a life-threatening condition associated with the antagonism of dopamine that presents with altered mental status, muscle rigidity or tremor, hyperthermia, and autonomic dysfunction. Common causative agents are antipsychotics (especia lly high-potency antipsychotics such as haloperidol) and antidopaminergic nausea medications. Rigidity and tremor result from dopamine antagonism in the nigrostriatal pathway, while autonomic dysfunction and hyperthermia may result from dopamine antagonism in the hypothalamus. Characteristic laboratory abnormalities include leukocytosis along with increased serum concentration of creatine kinase, lactate dehydrogenase, and alkaline phosphatase (as a result of prolonged muscle rigidity and consequent myolysis). Treatment is supportive and includes discontinuation of the offending medication, hydration, cooling blankets, and benzodiazepines if needed for agitation. Dantrolene is potentially beneficial.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Antibiotic-related fever (Choice A) is unlikely in this patient. While some antibiotics can cause mild increases in body temperature, marked hyperthermia is not a common side effect of antibiotic therapy. Furthermore, this patient is not current ly taking antibiotics. Herpes encepha litis (Choice B) presents with fever, altered mental status, and neurologic abnorma lities, such as seizure, aphasia, hemiparesis, or cranial nerve deficits. Neuroimaging will typically demonstrate changes in the tempora l lobe. Encephalitis is commonly associated with nuchal rigidity, which this patient does not demonstrate, making herpes encephalitis a less likely cause of his presentation. Additiona lly, an increased creatine kinase concentration is not consistent with herpes encephalitis. Lithium toxicity (Choice C) presents with nausea, vomiting, dysrhythmias, altered mental status, and neuromuscu lar excitability, such as tremors in acute toxicity. Chronic toxicity has more prominent neuro logic symptoms and can also cause nephrogenic diabetes insipid us. Malignant hyperthermia (Choice D) is caused by a genetic defect in the ryanodine receptor and presents with muscle rigidity, tachycardia, fever, lactic acidosis, and hypercarbia when the patient is exposed to succinylcholine or volatile anesthetics. While the presentation is similar to NMS, this patient has not been exposed to agents that trigger malignant hyperthermia since his surgery, making this a less likely cause of his illness. Postoperative sepsis (Choice F) presents with fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, and leukocytosis, as well as hypotension and lactic acidosis if the patient is in septic shock, in the setting of a known or suspected infection. It is rarely associated with hypertension. Furthermore, this patient has no signs of infection on physical examination. Educational Objective: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a life-threatening condition associated with the antagonism of dopamine that presents with altered mental status, muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, and autonomic dysfunction. Characteristic laboratory abnorma lities include leukocytosis along with increased concentrations of creatine kinase, alkaline phosphatase, and lactate dehydrogenase.

questionStem: A 32-year-o ld woman is brought to the emergency depart ment because of progress ive visual dimming in her right eye since awakening 8 hours ago. Her symptoms began with a mild headache over her right eye before going to bed last night. She says this headac he is different than her usual migraines that have improved since she started treatment with propranolol. Fundusco pic exam ination shows no abnorma lities of the right eye, but the patient cannot read and can barely count fingers with the right eye. Visua l acuity in the left eye is norma l. A CT scan of the head shows normal findings. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Optic neuritis results from autoimmune demyelinating inflammation of the optic nerve and presents in young, often female, patients with unilatera l vision loss and pain that is exacerbated with extraocular movements. Ocular examination demonstrates reduced visua l acuity and color vision, a relative afferent pupillary defect, and may demonstrate optic disc edema. Diagnosis is confirmed with MRI demonstrating hyperintensity of the optic nerve. Patients with optic neuritis are at increased risk for multiple sclerosis (MS), and optic neuritis is a common initial finding in patients with MS. Recently, autoantibodies against myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) and aquaporin-4 (AQP4) have been identified as causative of some cases of optic neuritis. Patients who develop optic neuritis as a result of antibodies against MOG and AQP4 often have severe presentations but also have decreased risk for subsequent MS compared to patients with optic neuritis who lack these autoantibodies. The Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial demonstrated that a short course of treatment with high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone speeds the rate of visual recovery and delays the onset of MS, although it does not impact final visual acuity, and demonstrated that the presence and quantity of periventricular white matter lesions on MRI is the most important prognostic risk factor for the subsequent development of MS.
incorrectExplanation: nd H. Diabetic retinopathy (Choice A) results from microvascular damage to retinal capillaries and is characterized by the presence of microaneurysms, intraretinal hemorrhages, and retinal nerve fiber layer infarctions. Diabetic retinopathy is usually symmetric between both eyes and is not painful.

questionStem: A previous ly healt hy 4 ?-year-o ld man is brought to the physician because of a 2-week history of progressive weakness. He says that during this period, his feet "flop" while walking, and he trips when walking up stairs. During the past week , he has had difficulty standing up from low chairs and open ing jars. He has not had pain or tingling. He has had constipation but no changes in bladder or sexual functio n. He has not had any recent infections or vaccinations. He takes no medications. He has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 20 years. He drinks three to four beers daily; for the past 6 weeks he has been drinking home-d istilled whiskey. Examination shows atrophy of the intrinsic muscles of the hands and feet. Muscle strength is 4/5 in the wrist and finger extensors, interosseous, iliopsoas, and hamstring muscles and 3/5 in the anterior tibialis, peronei, and posterior tibial is muscles. Deep te ndon reflexes are 1 + diffuse ly. Babinski sign is absent. Sensory examination shows no abnorma lities. Laboratory studies show microcytic anemia and hyperuricemia . Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's neurologic symptoms?
correctExplanation: Symptoms of acute lead poisoning occur within days or weeks of exposure and include abdominal pain, constipation, arthra lgia, myalgias, muscle weakness, excessive fatigue, headache, and difficulty concent rating. With prolonged exposure, chronic neurologic symptoms such as decline in cognition, depression, distal motor neuropathy, decreased hearing, tremor, and decreased brain volume on imaging may be present. The distal motor neuropathy causes lower motor neuron signs such as atrophy of muscles and hyporeflexia, as shown in this patient. Microcytic anemia is also common, since lead inhibits the enzymes ferrochelatase and o-ALA dehydratase, resulting in decreased heme synthesis. In adults, exposure to lead primarily comes through occupation and/or hobbies. Individuals working with batteries, mining, construction , or ammunition are at higher risk. Illegally distilling alcohol has a risk for lead toxicity because of the leaching of lead from solder in the still, which is likely where this patient received exposure. Diagnosis is suspected based on exposure and symptoms and confirmed with increased serum lead concentration. Management of lead poisoning depends on the blood lead concen tration and presence of symptoms, and includes chelation with dimercaprol, ethylene diamine tetraacetate, or succimer. Sources of lead should be investigated and eliminated.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Acute intermittent porphyria (Choice A) is an autosoma l dominant disorder caused by inactivating mutations of the enzyme porphobilinogen deaminase, resulting in deficient synthesis of heme and accumulation of porphobilinogen. Patients typically present during an acute attack with psychosis, abdominal pain, muscle weakness, neuropathy, and burgundy-colored urine. This patient's subacute presentation in the context of alcohol distillation is more consistent with lead poisoning.

questionStem: An 18-year-o ld man is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after he fell 25 feet. On examination, he is paraplegic and has urinary incontinence . Examination of the lower extremities shows absent reflexes and flaccid tone. Babinski sign is present bilaterally. X-rays of the spine show a fracture dislocat ion of T10. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's urinary incontinence?

choices.B: Compression of the S3-4 nerve roots
choices.C: Compression of the T10- 11 nerve roots
choices.D: Compression of the thoracic spinal cord

correctExplanation: An injury at the level of the thoracic spinal cord would affect the thoracic cord and may also affect segments distal to the level of the injury, including the lumbosacral segments that innervate lower extremity musculature and sensation. An injury at the level of T10 can affect sympathetic efferent fibers that provide inhibitory input to the bladder and urethra via the hypogastric nerve. Sympathetic stimulation through these fibers usually causes relaxation of bladder musculature and contraction of urethra l sphincter, resulting in urinary retention. Injury to these fibers will cause urinary incontinence as a result of impaired inhibition of bladder contraction. Spina l cord pathologies that result in urinary incontinence result in complex interactions between signals from the parasympathetic, sympathetic, and somatic nervous systems and may present with urge or overflow incontinence, altogether termed neurogenic bladder.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Compression of the conus medullaris (Choice A) often occurs at the level of L2. It can also present with sphincter dysfunction, spastic or flaccid paralysis, as well as saddle anesthesia. An injury at T10 would be unlikely to affect the conus medullaris. Compression of the S3-4 nerve roots (Choice B) describes cauda equina syndrome. Cauda equina syndrome presents with low back pain, weakness of lower extremities, bladder and rectal sphincter paralysis leading to urinary retention, and sensory deficits. Compression of the T10-11 nerve roots (Choice C) would result in a thoracic radiculopathy in a dermatomal distribution resulting in pain and numbness around the umbilicus. Rupture of the bladder neck (Choice E) would present with hematuria, pelvic pain, lower abdominal pain, and difficulty voiding. It would be unlikely to be the cause of the patient's urinary incontinence and would not present with lower extremity neurologic symptoms. questionStem: Four days after admission to the hospital for intravenous antibiotic therapy for a leg rash, a 77-year-old man is unable to urinate. The rash developed 10 days ago on his right foot and has now spread to his calf. On admission, the right lower extremity was warm and erythematous. Yesterday, he had the onset of neck pain. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus currently treated with glyburide. He appears acutely ill. His temperature is 39°C (102.2°F). Examination shows nuchal rigidity. The right lower extremity is warm and erythematous. Muscle strength is full in the proximal upper extremities and is 4/5 in the hands. He is unable to lift the lower extremities against gravity. Deep tendon reflexes are brisk. Babinski sign is present bilaterally. Sensation to pinprick is decreased below C?. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: An epidural abscess is a localized collection of pus in the epidural space between the dura mater and periosteum. It most commonly occurs in the spine but may occur in the brain. Most patients are elderly and have a history of concomitant infection and often have a history of immunocompromise (eg, diabetes mellitus, HIV infection, alcohol use disorder). Epidural abscess is more common in patients with a history of intravenous drug use. Infectious organisms usually spread to the epidural space hematogenously, from spinal surgery, or from adjacent osteomyelitis. Staphylococcus aureus is a frequent causative organism, but fungal infections also occur. Patients present with signs and symptoms of fever, altered mental status, meningismus, localized back pain and tenderness to palpation, and weakness, numbness, and paralysis below the affected spinal level. Treatment is with broad spectrum antibiotics and surgical drainage of the abscess.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Herniated cervical disc (Choice B) is caused by dislocation of the nucleus pulposus and annulus fibrosus of a cervical intervertebra l disc and may produce cervical radiculopathy or spinal cord compression. Patients present with neck pain and dermatomal arm pain and weakness. Infected hematoma of the spine (Choice C) may rarely occur following epidural hematoma formation in the spinal column. Patients often have a history of anticoagulation or coagulopathy plus immunocompromise or recent instrumentation. Meningitis (Choice D) may result from meningeal bacterial, viral, or fungal infection, and presents with feve r, meningismus and altered mental status. questionStem: An otherw ise healthy 52-year-old financia l advisor comes to the phys ician because of a 6-week history of progressive right hand weakness that is interfe ring with his ability to write. There is no history of trauma to the hand. He takes no medications. He is 180 cm (5 ft 11 in) tall and weighs 90 kg (199 lb); BMI is 28 kg/m2. Exami nation of the right hand shows decreased active abduction of the small and index fingers. He cannot cross and uncross his right index and middle fingers, and he is unable to pinch the palmar aspect of the right thumb against the radial side of the index finger without flexing the interphalangeal joint of the thumb to provide strength. Active flexion of the interphalangeal joints of the right hand is 5/5. Sensation over the entire dorsal aspect of the hand is normal. The rema inder of the neuro logic examinat ion shows no focal findings. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Electrophysiological studies are utilized to diagnose ulnar neuropathy. Ulnar neuropathy typically arises from ulnar nerve entrapment at the elbow or wrist, which may occur idiopathically or because of trauma, compression, or elbow joint pathology. While ulnar nerve entrapment at the elbow typically results in numbness and paresthesia of the medial hand and wrist, ulnar nerve entrapment at the wrist typical ly leads to weakness of the intrinsic hand muscles and the consequent loss of hand dexterity. The ulnar nerve innervates the palmaris brevis, hypothenar, lumbrica l, interossei, and adductor pollicis muscles. As a result of adductor pollicis dysfunction, patients illustrate a decreased ability to pinch the first two digits together. As a result of interossei muscle dysfunction, this patient is unable to fully abduct or adduct the digits. Sensory dysfunction in the ulnar distribution may result from ulnar entrapment at the wrist as well. Electrophysiological studies (eg, nerve conduction studie s or electromyography) confirm the clinical diagnosis. Management begins with conservative methods (eg, activity modification) but may include surgical decompression for severe or refractory symptoms.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. MRI of the brachia ! plexus (Choice A) would diagnose brachia! plexopathies. Brachia! plexopathies typically present with numbness, paresthesia, or weakness of the shoulder and arm, and less common ly, the hand. If present, intrinsic hand weakness is typically accompanied by forearm or shoulder weakness. MRI of the neck (Choice B) could identify cervica l radiculopathy. Cervical radiculopathy refers to cervical nerve root pathology that leads to weakness, numbness, paresthesia, and pain in the dermatomal distribution that corre lates to the affected nerve root. This patient's isolated intrinsic hand muscle weakness does not corre late with any dermatome.

questionStem: A 23-year-o ld woman with sickle cell disease is brought to the emergency department after becoming obtunded; she has a 2-day history of cough and fever. Her temperature is 39.3°C (102.7°F), pulse is 128/min, respirations are 28/min, and blood pressure is 98/60 mm Hg. She appears stuporous. She is intubated and mechanica lly ventilated. There is m1oderate nuchal rigidity. Right basilar crackles are heard on auscultat ion. Hematocrit is 21 % with many nucleated erythrocytes , and leukocyte count is 24,000/ mm 3. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.D: Transf usion of 3 units of packed red blood cells

correctExplanation: Bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, nuchal rigidity, and altered mental status, typical ly following a prodrome of upper respiratory tract infection symptoms, although it can also be concomitant with another infection. Physical examination may disclose a present Kernig or Brudzinski sign, indicative of meningeal irritation, and can also demonstrate focal neurologica l symptoms or signs of increased intracranial pressure, such as hemiparesis or abducens nerve palsy. Petechiae may be present. Laboratory evaluation will show leukocytosis, and coagulation studies can show signs of disseminated intravascular coagulopathy with thrombocytopenia, decreased fibrinogen, and increased d-dimer, depending on the specific pathogen. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) evaluation is the initial diagnostic step and will reveal an increased opening pressure, increased leukocyte count with prominent neutrophi ls, increased protein concentration, and decreased glucose concentration. Culture of the CSF is utilized to diagnose the specific bacteria l cause and to distinguish between viral and fungal meningitides, or alternative diagnoses. The most common causes of bacterial meningitis in patients with asplenia, whether functiona l or operative, are Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis. Treatment involves immediate antibiotic therapy, accompanied by glucocorticoids.

This patient is likely septic, given her tachycardia, tachypnea, fever, and leukocytosis. She is mildly hypotensive, and administration of intravenous fluids and antibiotics is the most important immediate therapy. Norepinephrine is a more appropriate initial vasopressor used to treat septic shock. CT scan of the head (Choice C) may be utilized in the evaluation of bacterial meningitis. questionStem: A 57-year-o ld man comes to the physician because of progressive weakness in both legs over the past 5 months. He has trouble arising from a chair and climbing stairs; he finds it easier to arise from a chair if he rocks back and forth first. During this time, he has also had a persistent cough, a 14-kg (30-lb) weight loss, and a dry mouth. He has smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 40 years. Exami nation shows weakness of hip flexion and knee extens ion. There is no muscle tenderness . All reflexes are absent. Babinski sign is absent. Sensory examination shows no abnorma lities. His erythrocyte sedimentat ion rate is 95 mm/h, and serum creatine kinase activity is 25 U/L. An x-ray of the chest shows a right upper lobe mass. Which of the following is the most likely location of the abnorma lity?
correctExplanation: Myasthenic (Lambert-Eaton) syndrome is an uncommon neurologic condition that affects neuromuscu lar junction transmission. Normally, action potentials lead to depolarization in the termina l bouton of the axon. Voltage-gated calcium channels consequently open and allow calcium influx, which triggers the exocytosis of neurotransmitter-fil led vesicles into the synaptic cleft. Patients with myasthenic (Lambert-Eaton) syndrome possess antibodies to voltage-gated calcium channe ls on presynaptic lower motor neurons, which decreases calcium influx and acety lcholine release to postsynaptic skeletal muscle cells. This patient with a smoking history, persistent cough, weight loss, and increased erythrocyte sedimentation rate likely has small cell lung cancer and paraneoplastic autoantibody production against voltage-gated calcium channe ls, causing myasthenic (Lambert-Eaton) syndrome. Patients consequent ly demonstrate progressive proxima l muscle weakness with depressed or absent deep tendon reflexes. The muscle weakness typica lly improves with exercise as sma ll amounts of acety lcholine accumulate in the synaptic cleft over time, increasing the frequency of postsynaptic action potentials in skeletal muscle cells. Autonomic symptoms such as decreased salivation (and consequent dry mouth) may also occur. The diagnosis may be confirmed with nerve conduction studies and electromyography with exercise testing.
incorrectExplanation: nd F. Anterior horn cell (Choice A) degeneration can be caused by poliovirus infection, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or spinal muscu lar atrophy (a congenital disease presenting with progressive anterior horn disease). Patients would present with a lower-motor neuron pattern of weakness with decreased reflexes. However, anterior horn cell disease is not associated with lung cancer.

questionStem: A 52-year-o ld man who is HIV positive is brought to the physician by his mother because of a 1-month history of forgetfulness and inappropriate behavior. He also has been buying numerous items from the Internet. He also has had diarrhea. During the past year, he has been noncompl iant with his antiretroviral medication regimen and has had a 16-kg (35-lb) weight loss. He is 173 cm (5 ft 8 in) tall and weighs 46 kg (101 lb); BMI is 15 kg/m2. His temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F), pulse is 98/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 110/60 mm Hg. Examination shows thrush. On mental status examination, he has a labile affect. He recalls zero of three objects after 5 minutes. A CT scan of the head shows prominent atrophy of the cortex and demyelination in the subcortica l white matter. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is a life-threatening demyelinating disease that occurs as a result of the reactivation of human polyomavirus 2 (former ly JC virus) in patients who are immunocompromised. Most people experience an asymptomatic infection with human polyomavirus 2 during childhood, at which point the virus becomes latent. In severely immunocompromised patients, human polyomavirus 2 can reactivate and infect oligodendrocytes, leading to demyelination. Patients typically present with the subacute onset of focal neurologic deficits related to the affected brain area and cognitive impairment. Patients who are immunocompromised enough to have PML may also present with symptoms of other opportunistic infections. This patient's thrush and potential Mycobacterium avium complex infection (which likely explains his fever, diarrhea, and weight loss) indicate severe immune compromise in the setting of decreased adherence to antiretroviral therapy. MRI may demonstrate unilateral or bilateral white matter lesions without mass effect indicative of demyelination, which may progress to cortical atrophy. Lumbar puncture and cerebrospina l fluid analysis confirm the diagnosis. Treatment requires restarting antiretroviral therapy.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Central nervous system lymphoma (Choice A), or primary CNS lymphoma, is a rare variant of non-Hodgkin lymphoma that occurs most common ly in immunocompromised patients. Typical presentation includes focal neurological deficits, neuropsychiatric symptoms, or signs of increased intracranial pressure (eg, positional headache, nausea, vomiting). MRI typically demonstrates a solitary mass lesion but can reveal multiple periventricular white matter mass lesions. Primary CNS lymphoma lesions do not involve demyelination and are more likely to produce a mass effect than PML lesions. Dementia, Alzheimer type (Choice B) results from decreased cholinergic signaling in the cortex and basal forebrain. Alzheime

correctExplanation: This patient presenting with an upper motor neuron pattern of dysfunction in the lower extremities and a lower motor neuron-pattern of dysfunction in the upper extremities likely has syringomyelia. Syringomyelia features a progressively expanding cystic lesion involving midline spinal cord structures. Syringomyelia may be associated with congenital malformations such as Chiari type I malformation, spinal cord infections, autoimmune diseases such as multiple sclerosis, neoplasms, or spinal cord trauma. Syringomyelia typically damages spinothalamic fibers decussating in the anterior white commissure. Consequent ly, patients present with deficits in pain and temperature sensation in the bilateral upper extremities (since the ascending spinothalamic tracts in the lateral spinal cord are unaffected, sensation in the lower body is intact). The spinothalamic tract also carries sensory fibers that mediate poorly localized light touch (versus localized light touch fibers of the posterior columns). The cystic lesion can expand to the bilateral anterior horns (the location of the cell bodies of lower motor neurons). Therefore, patients may also present with a lower motor neuron pattern of dysfunction in the bilateral upper extremities (eg, decreased muscle tone, hyporeflexia, early muscle atrophy). The cyst may also progressive ly expand to the lateral corticospinal tract in severe cases, leading to an upper motor neuron pattern of dysfunction (eg, spastic weakness, hyperreflexia, positive Babinski sign) in the lower body.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Choice A) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder that affects the anterior horns along with the lateral corticospinal tract as it descends in the brain and spinal cord. Subsequently, patients demonstrate a combination of upper and lower motor neuron findings in an asymmetric distribution that may include the bulbar muscles. Sensory impairment would be atypical, and a pattern of dysfunction that can be localized to a single lesion within the cervical spine is more consistent with syringomyelia. questionStem: A 77-year-o ld woman is brought to the physician by her husba nd because of a 3-day history of visua l difficult ies. He says she seems a little "off balance." She agreed to come in after dent ing the car on the left side while parking it in the garage. She has not had any headaches or noticed any difficulty using either side of her body. She has not fallen recently. She has a 2-year history of atrial fibril lation treated with aspirin. She is sitting comfortab ly in a chair. Her temperatu re is 37°C (98.6 °F), pulse is 95/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 110/80 mm Hg. Examination shows a left homonymous hemianopia . Muscle strength, muscle tone, and sensation are intact bilatera lly. Speech is normal. She is alert and oriented to person, place, and time . When asked to read, she only reads the words on the right side of the page. A CT scan of the head is most likely to show an infarct in the territory of which of the following cerebra l arteries?
correctExplanation: Occlusion of the right posterior cerebra l artery (PCA) explains this patient's deficits. The PCA supplies much of the occipital lobes as well as the inferomedial temporal lobe, posteromedial parietal lobe, thalamus, and parts of the brainstem. Visual symptoms are a prominent feature of a PCA territory infarction and include cortical blindness, contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing, visua l agnosia, and prosopagnosia. Occlusion of the right PCA typically leads to left homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing (caused by damage of the right primary visua l cortex) and may lead to left hemineglect (caused by damage of the right parieta l cortex). Left homonymous hemianopia likely explains this patient's car accident and may lead to mild balance difficulties. Occlusion of the right PCA may also result in left hemisensory deficit (caused by thalamus damage) and left hemiparesis (caused by damage to the cerebral peduncles in the midbrain). Cerebral infarctions, also known as strokes, occur as a result of ischemic or hemorrhagic loss of blood supply to the brain. Approximately 80% to 85% of strokes are ischemic, commonly arising from thromboembolic disease (eg, middle cerebral artery occlusion from a thrombus), whereas 15% to 20% of strokes are hemorrhagic because of blood vessel rupture (eg, hypertension-related intraparenchymal hemorrhage from a perforating artery). Risk factors for stroke include smoking, hypertension, diabetes, carotid or intracranial atherosclerotic disease, history of hypercoagulabi lity, atrial fibrillation, and advanced age. Classically, strokes manifest as a neurologic deficit related to the affected part of the brain.

questionStem: A 72-year-o ld woman is brought to the physician 2 hours after the sudden onset of dim vision in her right eye. Her symptoms began 3 weeks ago with genera lized stiffness, aches in the morning, and a bitemporal headac he. Examination shows firm , tender temporal arteries bilateral ly. Corrected visual acuity is 20/200 in the right eye and 20/40 in the left. Laboratory studies show: Hematocrit Leukocyte count Platelet count Erythrocyte sedimentation rate Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?

choices.B: Aspirin therapy now and temporal artery biopsy within 24 hours
choices.C: Corticosteroid therapy now and temporal artery biopsy within 3 days
choices.E: Temporal artery biopsy now with therapy determined by pathology

correctExplanation: 32% 6000/mm 3 300,000/mm 3 110 mm/h This patient's presenting findings of abrupt onset monocular vision loss, headache, stiffness, and temporal tenderness are consistent with a diagnosis of giant cell arteritis (GCA). GCA is an autoimmune inflammatory vasculitis of medium and large vesse ls. Classic findings include systemic symptoms of fever, chills, and weight loss, headache, history of preceding transient vision loss (amaurosis fugax), jaw claudication, tenderness of the scalp, and pale optic disc edema. New headaches in an elderly patient should raise suspicion for GCA. GCA frequent ly occurs in association with polymyalgia rheumatica, which is characterized by stiffness of proximal muscles. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates increased inflammatory markers, including erythrocyte sedimentation rate and C-reactive protein concentration, and thrombocytosis. GCA is characterized by a predilection for the vesse ls of the head and neck, and often affects the ophthalmic artery, inflammatory occlusion of which can result in sudden, ischemic damage to the retina. Once vision loss occurs it is not reversible and is commonly followed by vision loss in the contralatera l eye within days or weeks. The diagnosis is confirmed with biopsy of the tempora l artery demonstrating granulomatous vasculitis. Treatment with high dose corticosteroids should occur immediately once GCA is suspected in order to preserve vision. Corticosteroid treatment does not generally compromise biopsy results as long as the biopsy is performed within 1 to 2 weeks.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Carotid angiography (Choice A) is not a preferred diagnostic method for the detection of GCA. Temporal artery biopsy remains the standard diagnostic test. Steroid treatment should not be deferred while pursuing other tests.

questionStem: A previous ly healthy 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her brother 1 hour after a generalized tonic-clonic seizure that lasted 5 minutes. The patient and her brother emigrated from Central America 6 months ago. She takes no medications. She is drowsy but cooperative. Her temperature is 37.1 °C (98.8°F), pulse is 80/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 150/90 mm Hg. Examination and laboratory studies show no other abnorma lities. Toxicology screening is negative . A CT scan of the head with contrast is shown. Which of the following is the most likely diagnos is?
correctExplanation: Neurocysticercosis is a central nervous system (CNS) infection caused by the pork tapeworm Taenia so/ium that occurs most common ly in endemic rural regions of Latin America, Asia, and Africa. Symptoms include headache, seizures, signs of increased intracranial pressure, and, rarely, altered vision. Certain patients are asymptomatic, and other patients present with muscle or subcutaneous nodules. Typical manifestations on CT or MRI include cystic, ring-enhancing, calcified lesions in the brain parenchyma, meninges, ventricles, spinal cord, or orbit. A scolex (larval head) may also be demonstrated on imaging. Treatment may include symptomatic management of increased intracranial pressure and seizures, antiparasitic therapy, or steroids.
